top: Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine, butyrate, TCA intermediates). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't do that, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.
glutamine: L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)) is the main fuel for your enterocytes, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It skips the complicated digestive steps other nutrients have to go through. Inside the mitochondria it gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG), which feeds the citric acid cycle, where the mitochondria make their energy. So the cells get that energy right away, and that's what drives the repair of the gut lining and keeps LPS from slipping through.
dosing: Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.
caution: CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active colon or liver cancer, don't raise the dose that high. The liver is on that list because it's where the glutamine goes first, through the portal vein.
butyrate: Butyrate and the other short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are what your colon runs on, the way your small intestine runs on glutamine. You get them when your gut bacteria ferment raw resistant starch, or from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt. They feed the colonocytes and tighten up the lower gut barrier, and they keep turning down inflammatory signals too.
tca: TCA cycle intermediates, like malic and citric acid, are organic acids that go directly into the same energy pathways in the mitochondria that glutamine does. So clean sour stuff like organic malic acid, tart cherries or green apples gives the cells lining your gut another quick fuel, and it speeds up healing of the lining, just by a different biochemical route than glutamine.
